Let
\[
T_i=cI+sJ_i,\qquad s=\sqrt{1-c^2}.
\]
The condition \(\langle x,T_i x\rangle=c\|x\|^2\) says the symmetric part of \(T_i\) is \(cI\). Since \(T_i\) is orthogonal, each \(J_i\) is skew-symmetric and satisfies
\[
J_i^2=-I.
\]
So each \(J_i\) is an orthogonal complex structure on \(\mathbb R^4\).

For \(i\ne j\),
\[
T_iT_j=c^2I+cs(J_i+J_j)+s^2J_iJ_j.
\]
The middle term is skew-symmetric, so comparing symmetric parts with the condition
\[
\langle x,T_iT_jx\rangle=c\|x\|^2
\]
gives
\[
\frac{J_iJ_j+J_jJ_i}{2}=\frac{c-c^2}{1-c^2}I=\frac{c}{1+c}I.
\]
Set
\[
a=\frac{c}{1+c}.
\]
Then
\[
J_iJ_j+J_jJ_i=2aI.
\]

Now use the standard inner product on skew matrices
\[
\langle A,B\rangle=-\frac14\operatorname{tr}(AB).
\]
Each \(J_i\) has norm \(1\), and taking traces in the anticommutator identity gives
\[
\langle J_i,J_j\rangle=-a\qquad (i\ne j).
\]

In dimension \(4\), orthogonal complex structures split into two \(3\)-dimensional families, according to orientation. If two are from opposite families, their above inner product is \(0\). Since here \(-a\ne0\), all four \(J_i\) lie in the same \(3\)-dimensional Euclidean space.

Thus we have four unit vectors in a \(3\)-dimensional Euclidean space with constant pairwise inner product \(-a\). Their Gram matrix has diagonal \(1\) and off-diagonal \(-a\). Its eigenvalues are
\[
1+a \quad\text{with multiplicity }3,\qquad 1-3a \quad\text{with multiplicity }1.
\]
Because four vectors lie in a \(3\)-dimensional space, the Gram matrix is singular, so
\[
1-3a=0.
\]
Hence
\[
a=\frac13.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{c}{1+c}=\frac13,
\]
so
\[
3c=1+c,\qquad 2c=1,\qquad c=\frac12.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac12}
\]
